questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with Clostridioides difficile infection. Which action by the nurse requires correction?

options.text: Puts on a gown and gloves before entering the room
Uses a dedicated stethoscope that stays in the room
Cleans hands with alcohol-based hand rub after leaving the room
Cleans the bedside table with a bleach-based disinfectant

rationale.correct: C. difficile forms spores that resist alcohol, so soap-and-water handwashing is required after care.

perOption.a: Contact precautions require a gown and gloves for any contact with the client or the environment.
perOption.b: Dedicated equipment prevents spores from spreading to other clients.
perOption.c: Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores; hands must be washed with soap and water, which removes the spores mechanically.
perOption.d: A sporicidal (bleach-based) disinfectant is recommended for C. difficile.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Use soap and water, not alcohol rub, after caring for a client with C. difficile.

questions.stem: A client is admitted with suspected active pulmonary tuberculosis. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Place the client in an airborne infection isolation (negative-pressure) room
Wear a fit-tested N95 respirator when entering the room
Keep the door to the room closed
Have the client wear a surgical mask when leaving the room for tests
Wear a surgical mask instead of a respirator when giving brief care
Place the client in a semi-private room with another client who has TB pneumonia

rationale.correct: TB spreads by airborne droplet nuclei, so airborne precautions are needed: negative-pressure room, N95 respirator, closed door and a mask on the client during transport.

perOption.a: Negative pressure keeps airborne droplet nuclei from leaving the room.
perOption.b: An N95 filters the small particles that carry M. tuberculosis.
perOption.c: A closed door keeps the room under negative pressure.
perOption.d: A mask on the client contains respiratory secretions during transport.
perOption.e: A surgical mask does not filter airborne particles; a respirator is needed for every entry.
perOption.f: Clients with suspected TB need a single airborne isolation room; strains and drug resistance may differ.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Apply airborne precautions for suspected tuberculosis.

questions.stem: Which client should the nurse place on droplet precautions?

options.text: A client with a methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) wound infection
A client with pertussis
A client with measles (rubeola)
A client with scabies

rationale.correct: Droplet precautions (surgical mask within close range, private room) are used for pertussis, influenza, mumps, rubella and meningococcal disease.

perOption.a: MRSA spreads by contact; it needs contact precautions.
perOption.b: Pertussis spreads through large respiratory droplets; droplet precautions are required.
perOption.c: Measles is airborne and needs an airborne infection isolation room.
perOption.d: Scabies spreads by direct skin contact; it needs contact precautions.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify infections that need droplet precautions.

questions.stem: For each condition, indicate the type of transmission-based precautions the nurse should use in addition to standard precautions.

rationale.correct: Remember 'My Chicken Has TB' for airborne (measles, chickenpox, disseminated herpes zoster, TB); droplet for influenza, mumps, pertussis, rubella and meningococcus; contact for C. difficile, MRSA, VRE, scabies and lice.

perOption.r1:c1: Measles virus stays suspended in the air and needs airborne precautions.
perOption.r1:c2: Droplet precautions do not protect against the airborne measles virus.
perOption.r1:c3: Contact precautions alone do not stop airborne spread.
perOption.r2:c1: Influenza is not routinely airborne except during aerosol-generating procedures.
perOption.r2:c2: Influenza spreads by large droplets within about 2 m (6 ft).
perOption.r2:c3: Contact is a minor route; droplet precautions are required.
perOption.r3:c1: C. difficile is not spread through the air.
perOption.r3:c2: C. difficile is not spread by respiratory droplets.
perOption.r3:c3: Spores spread on hands and surfaces, so contact precautions are needed.
perOption.r4:c2: Mumps spreads by respiratory droplets and saliva.
perOption.r4:c3: Contact precautions alone are not enough.
perOption.r5:c1: TB spreads through airborne droplet nuclei.
perOption.r5:c2: A surgical mask and droplet precautions do not filter TB particles.
perOption.r5:c3: TB is not spread by contact.
perOption.r6:c2: Scabies is not spread by droplets.
perOption.r6:c3: Scabies spreads by skin-to-skin contact and shared linen.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to enter the room of a client on contact and droplet precautions. Place the steps for putting on personal protective equipment in order.

items.text: Put on gloves, pulling the cuffs over the gown sleeves
Put on goggles or a face shield

rationale.correct: CDC order for putting on PPE: hand hygiene, gown, mask or respirator, eye protection, gloves.

perOption.a: Clean hands come first so the PPE is not contaminated.
perOption.b: The gown goes on first so the mask ties and gloves can go over it.
perOption.c: The mask is placed before eye protection so the face shield or goggles fit over it.
perOption.d: Eye protection goes over the mask.
perOption.e: Gloves go on last and cover the gown cuffs to protect the wrists.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.stem: The nurse is leaving the room of a client on droplet and contact precautions while wearing a gown, gloves, goggles and a mask. Which item should the nurse remove last, just before performing hand hygiene?

options.text: Gloves
Goggles
Gown
Mask

rationale.correct: Removal order: gloves, goggles or face shield, gown, mask or respirator, then hand hygiene. This order removes the most contaminated items first.

perOption.a: Gloves are the most contaminated item and are removed first.
perOption.b: Eye protection is removed after gloves, handled by the clean headband or earpieces.
perOption.c: The gown is removed after the goggles (or together with the gloves), before the mask.
perOption.d: The mask is removed last, by the ties or ear loops, outside the room, followed by hand hygiene.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.stem: The nurse observes a student setting up a sterile field for a dressing change. Which action requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Opens the first flap of the sterile package away from the body
Keeps sterile gloved hands above waist level
Turns away from the sterile field to get extra gauze from the cart
Considers the 2.5 cm (1 inch) border of the sterile drape contaminated

rationale.correct: A sterile field must stay in view at all times; turning away breaks sterile technique because contamination can't be ruled out.

perOption.a: Opening the first flap away from the body avoids reaching over the sterile field.
perOption.b: Items below the waist are considered contaminated, so hands are kept above it.
perOption.c: A sterile field out of view is considered contaminated; the student must keep facing the field.
perOption.d: The outer 1 inch border of a sterile field is considered unsterile.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for an older adult client at high risk for falls. Which interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the bed in its lowest position with the wheels locked
Place the call light and personal items within reach
Raise all four side rails at night
Offer toileting assistance on a regular schedule
Provide nonskid socks or footwear
Keep the room completely dark at night to promote sleep

rationale.correct: Fall prevention combines a safe environment (low bed, night light, items in reach) with planned help (scheduled toileting, nonskid footwear), not restraint.

perOption.a: A low, locked bed reduces the distance and injury if a fall happens.
perOption.b: Reaching for items is a common cause of falls.
perOption.c: Four raised rails count as a restraint and increase injury when clients climb over them.
perOption.d: Scheduled toileting prevents rushed, unassisted trips to the bathroom.
perOption.f: A night light helps the client see when getting up; darkness increases fall risk.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: The nurse is supervising assistive personnel (AP) caring for a client in soft wrist restraints. Which action by the AP requires immediate correction?

options.text: Ties the restraint to the movable side rail
Uses a quick-release knot
Checks that two fingers fit under the restraint
Removes one restraint at a time to provide range of motion

rationale.correct: Restraints are secured to the bed frame (the part that moves with the bed), never the side rail, using a quick-release knot.

perOption.a: Raising or lowering a side rail can pull the restraint and injure the client; restraints are tied to the bed frame.
perOption.b: A quick-release knot allows rapid removal in an emergency.
perOption.c: Two fingers' space prevents impaired circulation while keeping the restraint secure.
perOption.d: Releasing one limb at a time allows skin care and range of motion while keeping the client safe.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client who keeps pulling at a nasogastric tube is confused. The provider writes, "Apply soft wrist restraints PRN for agitation." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Apply the restraints whenever the client becomes agitated
Contact the provider to clarify the order
Ask the client's family for consent to restrain
Apply the restraints and document the order as received

rationale.correct: Regulations prohibit PRN restraint orders; each order must be time-limited and renewed after the client is reassessed. Less restrictive measures should be tried first.

perOption.a: PRN restraint orders are not permitted.
perOption.b: Restraint orders must be time-limited and specific; PRN restraint orders are not allowed, so the order needs clarification.
perOption.c: Family consent does not replace a valid, time-limited provider order.
perOption.d: Acting on an invalid order puts the client and the nurse at risk.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: The nurse needs to use a portable fire extinguisher on a small wastebasket fire. Place the steps in order.

items.text: Sweep the nozzle from side to side
Aim the nozzle at the base of the fire

rationale.correct: PASS: Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep. The extinguisher is used only after the RACE steps (rescue, alarm, contain) for a small, contained fire.

perOption.a: The pin locks the handle; it must be removed first.
perOption.b: Aiming at the base puts out the fuel source, not just the flames.
perOption.c: Squeezing the handle releases the extinguishing agent.
perOption.d: A sweeping motion covers the whole base of the fire.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: The nurse is triaging victims at a mass-casualty incident using the START system. Which victim should the nurse tag red (immediate)?

options.text: A victim who walks to the treatment area with a forearm laceration
A victim with a respiratory rate of 36/min and capillary refill of 3 seconds
A victim who is not breathing after the airway is repositioned
A victim with a closed femur fracture who follows commands, with a respiratory rate of 20/min and capillary refill under 2 seconds

rationale.correct: In mass-casualty triage, the most resources go to victims who are critically injured but likely to survive with immediate care.

perOption.a: A victim who can walk is tagged green (minor).
perOption.b: A respiratory rate over 30/min or capillary refill over 2 seconds meets the criteria for immediate (red).
perOption.c: No breathing after the airway is opened is tagged black (expectant/deceased).
perOption.d: Stable breathing, perfusion and mental status with an injury that can wait is tagged yellow (delayed).

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: A disaster has been declared and the hospital needs beds for incoming casualties. Which client is most appropriate for the nurse to recommend for early discharge?

options.text: A client 2 days after an appendectomy who is walking and tolerating a regular diet
A client with heart failure receiving IV furosemide whose crackles are increasing
A client admitted 6 hours ago with diabetic ketoacidosis on an insulin infusion
A client with a new chest tube for a pneumothorax

rationale.correct: During a disaster, stable clients with predictable recovery are discharged first to free beds.

perOption.a: This client is stable, recovering as expected and can continue recovery at home.
perOption.b: Worsening crackles show the client is not stable.
perOption.c: An insulin infusion needs hourly monitoring in hospital.
perOption.d: A new chest tube needs ongoing inpatient monitoring.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: A client with a sealed cervical radiation implant calls the nurse and says, "Something fell out into the bed." The nurse sees the implant on the sheet. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Pick up the implant with gloved hands and place it in the trash
Use long-handled forceps to place the implant in the lead container in the room
Reinsert the implant into the applicator
Leave the room and close the door until the radiation safety officer arrives

rationale.correct: Time, distance and shielding protect against radiation. A dislodged sealed source is moved with long-handled forceps into the lead container kept in the room, then the team is notified.

perOption.a: Gloves do not protect against radiation, and a radioactive source must never go in regular trash.
perOption.b: Forceps add distance and the lead container provides shielding; both limit radiation exposure.
perOption.c: Only the radiation oncology team repositions implants.
perOption.d: Leaving the source exposed in the bed continues the client's exposure; it is contained first, then the radiation safety officer is notified.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to give IV chemotherapy. Which personal protective equipment should the nurse wear?

options.text: Clean examination gloves only
Two pairs of chemotherapy-tested gloves and a disposable, impermeable gown
A surgical mask and sterile gloves
A cloth gown and one pair of nitrile gloves

rationale.correct: Chemotherapy agents can be absorbed through the skin; double chemo-tested gloves and an impermeable gown are required, plus eye and face protection when splashing is possible.

perOption.a: Single standard gloves do not protect enough against hazardous drugs.
perOption.b: Hazardous-drug guidance calls for double chemotherapy-tested gloves and an impermeable gown that closes in the back.
perOption.c: Sterile gloves are not tested against chemotherapy agents, and a mask alone does not protect the skin.
perOption.d: Cloth gowns absorb hazardous drugs instead of blocking them.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: Before giving a medication, which method should the nurse use to identify the client?

options.text: Check the room number and the name on the door
Ask "Are you John Smith?"
Compare the client's stated name and date of birth with the identification band and the medication record
Ask the client's roommate to confirm the client's name

rationale.correct: The Joint Commission requires at least two client identifiers (such as name and date of birth), never the room number.

perOption.a: Room numbers and door signs change and are not client identifiers.
perOption.b: Confused or hard-of-hearing clients may say yes to any name.
perOption.c: Two identifiers checked against the band and the record meet the safety standard.
perOption.d: Another person is not a reliable identifier.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: The nurse realizes that a client received 10 units of regular insulin instead of the prescribed 1 unit. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Complete an incident (variance) report
Check the client's blood glucose and assess for signs of hypoglycemia
Notify the nurse manager
Document the error in the client's medical record

rationale.correct: After a medication error, assess the client first, then notify the provider, intervene as ordered, document the facts and complete an incident report.

perOption.a: The report is required, but the client's safety comes first.
perOption.b: Assessing the client for harm is the first priority after any medication error.
perOption.c: The manager is informed after the client is assessed and the provider is notified.
perOption.d: The facts of the event and the client's condition are charted after the client is assessed and treated.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: The nurse finds a client sitting on the floor beside the bed. After assessing the client, which entry should the nurse write in the medical record?

options.text: "Client fell out of bed because the side rail was down. Incident report completed."
"Found client sitting on floor next to bed at 0215. States, 'I was going to the bathroom.' No visible injuries. Provider notified."
"Client fell due to confusion. Should have been watched more closely."
"See incident report for details of the fall."

rationale.correct: Chart only objective facts and the care given; the incident report is a separate quality document and is not referred to in the chart.

perOption.a: The cause is assumed, and incident reports are never mentioned in the medical record.
perOption.b: This is objective and factual, includes the client's own words, the assessment and the notification.
perOption.c: Opinions and blame do not belong in the medical record.
perOption.d: Referring to the incident report makes it part of the record and removes its confidential, quality-improvement status.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: The nurse notices that the power cord of a client's IV infusion pump is frayed. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Wrap the frayed area with tape and keep using the pump
Replace the pump, label the damaged one and send it to biomedical engineering
Keep using the pump until the infusion is finished
Unplug the pump and run the infusion on battery power indefinitely

rationale.correct: Damaged electrical equipment is removed from use immediately, labeled and reported so no one else uses it.

perOption.a: Tape doesn't make a damaged cord safe; it remains an electrical hazard.
perOption.b: Faulty equipment is taken out of service, labeled and reported for repair.
perOption.c: Continued use risks shock or fire.
perOption.d: The pump still needs inspection, and the battery will run out.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: The home health nurse documents a first visit with an 82-year-old client who lives alone. Highlight the findings that are safety hazards.

segments.text: Throw rugs are placed in the hallway and kitchen
A space heater sits 30 cm (1 ft) from the bedroom curtains
Grab bars are installed beside the toilet and in the shower
Pills are kept in unlabeled containers on the counter
A working smoke detector is on each floor
The stairway light switch is only at the bottom of the stairs

rationale.correct: Home safety assessment focuses on fall hazards (rugs, poor lighting), fire hazards (space heaters) and medication safety.

perOption.s2: Loose rugs are a leading cause of tripping and falls in older adults.
perOption.s4: Space heaters need about 1 m (3 ft) of clearance from anything flammable.
perOption.s6: Grab bars reduce bathroom falls; they are protective.
perOption.s8: Unlabeled medications increase the risk of taking the wrong drug or dose.
perOption.s12: Climbing down dark stairs increases fall risk; switches are needed at both ends.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a client about home oxygen therapy. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I will post 'No Smoking' signs on my doors."
"I will store the spare tanks upright in a stand."
"I will keep my oxygen tank next to the gas stove so it's handy while I cook."
"I will use a water-based lubricant on my lips instead of petroleum jelly."

rationale.correct: Oxygen feeds fire, so keep it away from flames, heat and petroleum-based products, and don't smoke.

perOption.a: No Smoking signs warn visitors that oxygen is in use.
perOption.b: Securing tanks upright prevents them from falling and damaging the valve.
perOption.c: Oxygen supports combustion; tanks must be kept at least 1.5 to 3 m (5 to 10 ft) from open flames and heat sources.
perOption.d: Petroleum products are flammable near oxygen; water-based products are safe.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client begins having a generalized tonic-clonic seizure while sitting in a chair. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Put a padded tongue blade between the client's teeth
Hold the client's arms and legs to stop the movements
Ease the client to the floor and turn the client onto the side
Leave to get the emergency medication

rationale.correct: During a seizure: protect from injury, keep the airway open by turning to the side, never restrain or put anything in the mouth, and time the seizure.

perOption.a: Objects in the mouth can break teeth or block the airway.
perOption.b: Restraining a seizing client can cause fractures and soft-tissue injury.
perOption.c: Lowering the client prevents a fall, and the side-lying position keeps the airway open and lets secretions drain.
perOption.d: The nurse stays with the client and calls for help.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: The nurse is observing assistive personnel move clients. Which action requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Raises the bed to waist height before giving a bed bath
Bends at the waist to lift a box of supplies from the floor
Uses a friction-reducing sheet and a coworker to move a client up in bed
Stands with feet apart to widen the base of support

rationale.correct: Safe body mechanics: bend the knees, keep the back straight, hold loads close and use assistive devices.

perOption.a: Working at waist height reduces back strain.
perOption.b: Lifting with a bent back strains the spine; the AP should bend the knees and keep the back straight.
perOption.c: Friction-reducing devices and two staff reduce injury to the client and the staff.
perOption.d: A wide base of support improves balance.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A person wearing scrubs but no hospital identification badge enters a postpartum room and says, "I need to take the baby to the nursery for a test." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Let the person take the baby because they are wearing scrubs
Keep the newborn in the room with the mother and call security
Walk with the person to the nursery
Ask the mother whether she agrees to let the person take the baby

rationale.correct: Infant abduction prevention: only staff with the unit's special identification badge transport infants; anyone else is challenged and security is called.

perOption.a: Scrubs are easy to get; they don't prove a person is staff.
perOption.b: Staff without proper identification must not take an infant; the nurse protects the infant and activates the security plan.
perOption.c: Going along doesn't confirm the person's identity and still lets an unknown person handle the infant.
perOption.d: The mother can't verify staff identity either; the facility's security plan applies.

questions.stem: A client receiving chemotherapy has an absolute neutrophil count of 400/mm3. Select the 3 actions the nurse should take.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene before entering the room
Remove fresh flowers and plants from the room
Assign the client to a private room
Take the client's temperature rectally
Allow visitors with mild cold symptoms if they wear a mask
Place the client in a negative-pressure room

rationale.correct: An ANC under 500/mm3 means severe neutropenia and a high infection risk. Protective precautions keep pathogens away from the client.

perOption.a: Hand hygiene is the most effective way to prevent infection in a neutropenic client.
perOption.b: Flowers, plants and standing water can carry bacteria and fungi.
perOption.c: A private room reduces exposure to pathogens from other clients.
perOption.d: Rectal temperatures can injure the mucosa and introduce bacteria; they are avoided.
perOption.e: People with any infection should not visit a neutropenic client.
perOption.f: Negative pressure is for airborne infections; protective environments use positive pressure.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
